note: Five atoms: Greet Students at the Door · Restorative Interactions (formerly 2x10) · Co-Created Norms · Teach the Transition · The Repair Conversation. serves_concepts reflects vault row attachment, not exhaustive routing.

strategies.label: Greet Students at the Door
strategies.summary: Greeting students at the door is one example of an effective entry routine. The goal is not the greeting itself; the goal is creating a predictable transition from the hallway into learning.
solves: Unstructured transition time
Difficulty beginning class
Limited teacher-student connection
Lost instructional minutes
Lack of predictability
mechanism: Predictable routines reduce uncertainty — cognitive load drops
Students receive an immediate cue that learning has begun — attention shifts in
Teachers gather quick information before instruction
Positive interactions strengthen relationships and belonging
Entry becomes intentional rather than accidental
conditions: Students know what to do immediately after entering — routine taught
Bell work or an opening task is already prepared
Materials are accessible
Classroom expectations have been explicitly taught
Teacher can monitor both hallway and classroom

misconception.common: Standing at the door is often presented as best practice.
misconception.principle: Create a predictable, personal transition into learning.

implementations.label: Relational
implementations.description: Teacher greets every student by name and briefly checks in before directing them to the opening task.
best_fit: Teachers who enjoy conversation
Smaller classes

implementations.label: Procedural
implementations.description: Teacher greets students while directing them to begin a posted bell ringer.
best_fit: Teachers emphasizing efficient transitions
Larger classes

implementations.label: Low-Verbal
implementations.description: Teacher stands near the entrance, makes eye contact, smiles or nods, while students independently begin the entry routine.
best_fit: Teachers with quieter personalities
Students who thrive on predictable routines

adaptations: Morning meeting
Advisory
Secondary block schedule
Kindergarten welcome song
Student greeters
Digital check-in
Mood meter
Visual check-in

strategies.label: Restorative Interactions
strategies.summary: 2×10 is two minutes of non-academic conversation with one hard-to-reach student, held for ten school days running. The goal is not the ten conversations themselves; the goal is building a durable relationship with a student who is currently reachable only through the deed, not the person. Attributed to Raymond Wlodkowski; later popularized in Allen Mendler's Connecting with Students.
solves: A student who feels unseen or only-seen-when-in-trouble
Redirections that keep spending the bond instead of building it
A relationship that starts and stays in the negative
Escalating behavior with no relational channel to reach through
Limited one-on-one connection during a full teaching day
mechanism: Ten consecutive days signals reliability — the student learns the adult keeps coming back
Non-academic content means the interaction is not about compliance
Repeated positive contact builds relationship before the next hard moment
A felt sense of belonging conditions motivation
The channel engagement and feedback travel on gets stronger
conditions: The conversations stay genuinely non-academic — no schoolwork, no behavior talk
The teacher can protect two low-stakes minutes daily
Consistency across all ten days — a broken streak resets the signal
The teacher is curious about this student, not gathering leverage
The student is not put on the spot publicly

misconception.common: 2x10 is often presented as a behavior-fix trick.
misconception.principle: Build the relationship before you need it, on the student's terms, not the classroom's.

implementations.label: Conversational
implementations.description: Teacher initiates a brief, genuine chat about the student's interests — a game, a show, a weekend — following the student's lead each day.
best_fit: Teachers who connect easily through talk
Students who warm to verbal attention

implementations.label: Low-Verbal
implementations.description: Teacher uses short, repeated micro-contacts: noticing a shirt, a quick shared joke, a saved seat. Two minutes spread across small moments rather than one sit-down.
best_fit: Teachers with quieter styles
Students who find direct one-on-one talk intense

implementations.label: Interest-Anchored
implementations.description: Teacher opens with something from an interest survey or an observed hobby, and returns to that thread daily so the student sees continuity from one day to the next.
best_fit: Teachers who prefer a concrete starting point
Students who take time to trust that attention is real

adaptations: Split the two minutes across two staff who share the student
Advisory or homeroom slot
Written back-and-forth for students who prefer text to talk
Interest survey as a launch point
Extend past ten days when momentum is building
Team version: several teachers each run 2x10 with different students
Elementary morning check-in
Secondary hallway or transition contact
strategies.evidence_note: Wlodkowski's 85% improvement figure is practitioner-reported and illustrative, not a measured finding.
rp_connections: Relationship built before trouble is what lets correction land later
Naming the deed not the doer

strategies.label: Co-Created Norms
strategies.summary: Co-created norms are a class agreement authored with students. The goal is not the list on the wall; the goal is authorship. Students who help write the norms hold them, because they own them. This is where investment replaces compliance.
solves: Expectations that students follow but do not believe
Rules that feel imposed rather than shared
Weak buy-in when a teacher hands down a posted list
Norms that get ignored the moment the teacher looks away
A thin sense of belonging in the room's culture
mechanism: Authorship creates ownership — students hold norms they helped write
Investment replaces compliance: the agreement is theirs, so following it is self-consistency rather than obedience
Autonomy of authorship feeds motivation — voice in the rules raises the will to keep them (SoL Q4)
Shared, predictable expectations reduce extraneous cognitive load — students are not guessing what is allowed
Co-authorship is a pathway to belonging — helping name how the room treats each other is a way of belonging to it
conditions: Student voice is real, not decorative — their words actually make it onto the wall
Norms are few, simple, and positively stated
The agreement is revisited and revised, not signed once and forgotten
Enough relational trust exists that students will speak honestly
The teacher is willing to be bound by the agreement too

misconception.common: Let the students make the rules is often presented as the practice.
misconception.principle: Authorship creates ownership — students hold the norms they helped write.

implementations.label: K-2: Read-Aloud to Values
implementations.description: Teacher reads a picture book about friendship or fairness, then asks how the class wants the room to feel. Student answers become a short anchor chart, illustrated and signed.
best_fit: Early elementary
Teachers who anchor culture in story and image

implementations.label: Upper Elementary: Co-Drafted Agreement
implementations.description: Students brainstorm in small groups, the class clusters ideas into shared expectations, and everyone drafts and signs the agreement. Posted and revisited regularly.
best_fit: Grades 3-5
Teachers who want a durable, student-owned document

implementations.label: Middle School: Discussion of Why
implementations.description: Before writing anything, students discuss why norms matter — what a good room feels like, what erodes it. From that conversation they co-create and commit to the agreement.
best_fit: Grades 6-8
Teachers building motivation through reasoning and voice

adaptations: Advisory or morning meeting norm-setting
Group-work agreements for a single project
Digital collaborative draft
Norm revisit after a rough week
Student-facilitated norm review
Restorative circle to author or renew the agreement
Family or home input into the class values
sol_connections: Autonomy of authorship feeds Motivation (SoL Q4)
Predictable expectations reduce extraneous Cognitive Load
Working Memory freed for learning when the room is predictable
rp_connections: Co-created norms shift compliance to investment (Klevan 2021)

strategies.label: Teach the Transition
strategies.summary: A transition is taught and rehearsed the way content is taught — modeled, practiced, and named — rather than announced once and enforced afterward. The goal is not a quiet move between activities; the goal is a sequence students can run without holding it in their heads.
solves: The seam between activities is where most instructional time leaks — five minutes, five times a day, across a year
Students stall at the boundary not because they're refusing but because they don't know the next action
The teacher ends up narrating every move, which makes the class dependent on the narration
Noise and drift at the seam get read as a behavior tension when the source is structural
mechanism: A rehearsed sequence runs from memory rather than being assembled on the spot — working memory is freed for the work waiting on the other side of the move
Each rehearsal is a low-stakes retrieval of the sequence, which strengthens it — spaced and retrieval-based practice makes it durable
A known sequence narrows what attention has to track — one next action instead of a whole noisy room
Teaching the move in advance means the teacher shapes the moment rather than correcting after it, so relationships don't get spent on friction the design created
When students help build the sequence, they move through a structure they hold rather than one imposed on them
conditions: The steps are few and concrete enough to rehearse — the specific next action, not 'transition quietly'
There is time set aside to practice it when nothing is at stake, early, before it's needed under pressure
The signal is consistent — a cue that changes weekly has to be re-learned each time
The room supports it — materials where hands already are, a visible next step
The sequence gets re-rehearsed after breaks and when it degrades, rather than being re-announced louder

misconception.common: Often presented as getting students to move quickly and quietly.
misconception.principle: Students can only run a sequence they've practiced. Anything not rehearsed has to be assembled in the moment, and the moment is when there's least room to assemble it.

implementations.label: Rehearsed and named
implementations.description: Walk the sequence with students when nothing is happening: name the steps, model it, run it two or three times, name what made it work. Re-run it briefly after a long weekend.
best_fit: Early elementary
Any group meeting a new format

implementations.label: Student-built
implementations.description: Students draft the sequence themselves — what should this look like, what gets in the way, what's our signal — then rehearse their own version. Slower to install, holds better because they authored it.
best_fit: Upper elementary and middle
Any room where compliance is the current sticking point

implementations.label: Role-carried
implementations.description: Specific students carry the transition: caller, materials lead, timekeeper. The sequence travels through roles rather than through the teacher's voice.
best_fit: Students who struggle most at the seam — the role gives the regulation something to attach to

adaptations: K–2: attach the sequence to a song, chant, or counted signal; rehearse it as its own activity; pair it with a picture schedule
3–5: students manage their own materials and route inside the sequence; introduce a visible timer; rehearse the format change rather than each individual step
6–8: fewer steps, stated once, then handed over; students set the norm for what a clean move looks like; the sequence is between formats, not between tasks
After a disruption to the schedule — assembly, sub, testing week — rehearse rather than assume; the sequence degrades and re-teaching it is faster than correcting it
strategies.evidence_note: Kounin (1970) established momentum and smoothness — well-managed classrooms anticipate friction at activity boundaries rather than reacting to it. The widely repeated estimate that transitions cost ~75 hours of instructional time per year is practitioner-sourced and illustrative, not a measured finding.
sol_connections: Spaced retrieval-based practice makes sequences durable (SoL Q1/Q2)
Verbal + visual representation of steps outperforms either alone (SoL 2nd ed. 2026)
rp_connections: Predictable, co-held routines lower the need for correction (Klevan 2021)

strategies.label: The Repair Conversation
strategies.summary: A short, structured conversation after harm, built on four questions that surface what happened and what would make it right — held with each person separately first, then together when both are ready. The goal is not an apology; the goal is that the student stays inside the community that has to keep working after the incident.
solves: Something happened and the room can't just proceed as if it didn't
The available responses feel like a choice between letting it go and removing someone — neither addresses the harm
A forced apology gets produced and nothing about tomorrow is different
The student who caused harm leaves knowing they're in trouble but not what they'd do differently
mechanism: Who does the accounting: in a consequence the adult names the wrong; in a repair conversation the student constructs the account — that's the part that changes behavior
'What happened?' opens a story; 'Why did you do that?' invites a defense — the wording is doing the work
Naming who was affected makes the harm concrete and external, so the student looks at an impact rather than defending an identity
The student stays inside relationships and belonging, which is the channel any future correction has to travel through
The encounter itself generates the solidarity the agreement rests on — being heard, and hearing the other person (Why RJ Works, 2021)
conditions: Relationship is already banked — a repair conversation spends relational credit; if none was deposited, there's nothing to spend
Both people are regulated enough to talk — held too soon, it becomes a second incident
Each person is met separately first — the joint conversation only works if both arrive able to hear the other
The teacher can sit with silence and not fill it — most useful thinking happens in the pause after a question
The agreement reached is small enough to actually happen and gets followed up on

misconception.common: Often presented as the soft alternative to a consequence — talking it out instead of doing something.
misconception.principle: Harm is the problem to be addressed, not the person. The response has to keep the student inside the community that has to metabolize what happened.

implementations.label: The four questions
implementations.description: Held one-on-one: What happened? What were you thinking at the time? Who was affected, and how? What would make it right? Then the same four with the other person, then together.
best_fit: The standard case — two students, a clear incident, both able to talk

implementations.label: Separate-then-together (mediated)
implementations.description: Teacher works with each student individually first, building perspective-taking before either has to face the other, and only brings them together once both can hold the other's version.
best_fit: Conflicts with real heat in them
Where one student is much more verbal than the other

implementations.label: Low-verbal / written
implementations.description: Same four questions on paper or drawn, or answered one at a time across a day rather than in one sitting. Student responds in writing and teacher responds in writing back.
best_fit: Students who shut down under face-to-face questioning
Younger students
Anyone who needs processing time

adaptations: K–2: two questions, not four — what happened and what would help. Concrete restitution the child can physically do. A designated peace corner where the conversation happens.
3–5: all four questions, teacher-facilitated. Introduce the apology-of-action — doing something rather than saying something. Students begin holding these with light support.
6–8: students can facilitate for peers once they've been through several. Privacy matters more at this age — a repair conversation held where peers can watch will fail on audience alone.
Teacher-and-student repair: the same four questions when the rupture is between you and a student, including your own account. This is the version teachers skip and the one students remember.
strategies.evidence_note: Exclusionary discipline is associated with increased future misbehavior and dropout risk (Klevan 2021). Strongest caution in this literature is about fidelity, not efficacy: a restorative conversation run once after a blowup is not the same intervention as a practice running all year.
sol_connections: Feedback received through the relationship — the same words land as help or threat depending on what's already between teacher and student (SoL Q2)
Belonging conditions motivation; a student removed from community loses the precondition for engaging with the work (SoL Q4)
rp_connections: Harm met by restoring the relationship and preserving community, not by removal (Klevan 2021)
Why RJ Works (2021) — mechanism is the encounter itself: solidarity and emotional energy generated by being heard
